We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents the half-annulus between the disks of radii $3$ and $5$ centered at the origin. 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9,$ we obtain $r=3.$

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=25,$ we obtain $r=5.$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ The entire region lies between the radial lines $\theta =0$ and $\theta =\pi ,$ as depicted below.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14056707/assets/da18aafec278b5d44b0530097729e4cb4b319e219c005fc155d78fab8aa90937.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,3\le r\le 5,\,0\le \theta <\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{{x}^{2}y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{{r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{3}^{5}\frac{{r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{3}^{5}{r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{3}^{5}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (\frac{625}{4}-\frac{81}{4})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =136{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =136{[-\frac{{cos}^{3}⁡\theta }{3}]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =136\cdot (\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{272}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
